full_judgment:
2. Facts relevant are that a case under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was started on the basis of an application filed by opposite party No. 1 and a restraint order was issued by the learned Magistrate. The opposite party No. 1, thereafter, filed a petition before the self same Magistrate informing him that the accused petitioners violated the order issued under section 144 of the Code. The learned Magistrate sent the matter to the police authority of the thana for report. After enquiry the police submitted a report stating that the accused petitioners violated the said restraint order. The learned Magistrate then took cognizance against the accused petitioners under section 188 of the Penal Code. 

 3. Two grounds have been taken in this revisional application. The first is that the provisions of section 195(1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not followed and, as such, the proceedings could not be maintained. Secondly, the same Magistrate who issued order under section 144 of the Code cannot take cognizance under section 188 of the Penal Code for violation of his own order. 

 5. It has already been noticed that the order violated is an order under section 144 of the Code and the person aggrieved by the alleged violation, namely, the opposite party No.1, brought the same to the notice of the self same Magistrate who is competent to accept the complaint as well as take cognizance. A Magistrate passing a restraint order under section 144 of the Code is not ordinarily in a position to know that such order was violated unless the same is brought to his notice. In the instant case, as soon as the opposite party No.1 brought the violation to his notice he got the matter enquired by the police and on being satisfied that his order was violated he took cognizance against the petitioners. If the Magistrate passing the order under section 144 of the Code was different from the Magistrate competent to take cognizance then on being satisfied about the violation of his order he would be required to send a complaint in writing to the Magistrate competent to take cognizance. In such a circumstance cognizance taken by such a Magistrate on a complaint from any other person would have been illegal. On the other hand, had the learned Magistrate treated the information supplied by the opposite party No. 1 as a petition of complaint and took cognizance on the basis of that petition after examining him under section 200 of the Code then also it could be said that the learned Magistrate acted illegally in taking cognizance in violation of the bar under section 195(1) (a) of the Code. Neither circumstances being present in this case we find no merit in the first contention. 

 6. As regards the second contention, we find that the Magistrate who issued the order under section 144 of the Code is also the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance for an offence under section 188 of the Penal Code. In such a case we do not think that it is necessary that the same Magistrate is required to file a written complaint to him self Law does not require performance of an impossibility. If the officer to complain is the officer also to take cognizance then there is no necessity of filing a written complaint by the same officer to himself for taking cognizance of an offence against the accused persons So we find no merit in this contention also.
